senses.gloss: speaker, lecturer, interpreter; esp. Amora, one who, in lengthy popular discourses, expounds what the lecturer (Tanna, v. תַּנָּא) says before him in brief and in a low voice; often called מְתוּרְגְּמָן.
units: <cite ref="Shemot Rabbah 8">Ex. R. s. 8</cite>, end <he>כשם שהדורש … והא׳ וכ׳</he> as the lecturer sits … and the Amora speaks in his presence.—
<cite ref="Sanhedrin 7b:6">Snh. 7ᵇ</cite> <he>קום עליה בא׳</he> stand by him as an expounder.
<cite ref="Taanit 8a:12">Taan. 8ᵃ</cite>, a. fr. <he>אוקים … א׳ עליה ודרש</he> S. … placed an Amora by his side and lectured.
<cite ref="Sotah 40a:6">Sot. 40ᵃ</cite> <he>ואמר אֲמוֹרֵיה חד טעמא</he> and his Amora gave a different reason.
<cite ref="Chullin 15a">Ḥull. 15ᵃ</cite> do people listen to the Tanna? <he>לא׳ צייתי</he> they listen to the Amora.

senses.gloss: in a particular sense אֲמוֹרָא, Amora (Amoraïm), that class of Talmudic authorities who lived after the final redaction of the Mishnah, and whose discussions on the opinions of the Tannaïm or authors of the Mishnah and Boraitha, are deposited in the Guemara, thus adding a second element to the development of the oral law, called Talmud.—Pl. אֲמוֹרִין.
units: <cite ref="Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 1:1:15">Y. Ber. I, 2ᶜ</cite> top, a. e. <he>תרי א׳</he> two Amoraïm differ, for which Babli usually: … <he>אֲמוֹרָאֵי נינהו ואליבא</he> two Amoras differ in their relation (or conception) of the opinion of … <cite ref="Shevuot 40b:6">Shebu. 40ᵇ</cite>; a. fr.
